lesson.text: Quick memory: what was Skara Brae? (A New Stone Age village in Orkney, about 5,000 years old.) The same farming people built giant stone monuments.
Stonehenge in England is a circle of huge standing stones. It was built in stages: first a round ditch and bank about 3000 BC, then the giant stones were raised about 2500 BC.
The biggest stones, called sarsens, weigh about as much as four elephants each. They came from about 25 km away. The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, about 240 km away!
How, with no machines? Archaeologists think teams pulled the stones on wooden sledges with ropes, then levered them up into holes. Picks made of deer antler and stone hammers were found there.
The stones line up with the Sun: at midsummer the Sun rises near the Heel Stone, and at midwinter it sets in line with the stones. The builders watched the sky and the seasons carefully.

What archaeologists know: when the stones were raised, where they came from, and that people gathered and buried their dead there. Still a mystery: exactly why it was built, and how every stone was moved.
Stonehenge is not alone: there are more than 1,000 stone circles in Britain and Ireland. Avebury, not far away, is the biggest of all.
Try it in the world: build your own stone circle on a hill. Put one tall stone where the Sun rises in your world and watch the sunrise line up with it!

choices: a circle of huge standing stones
exercises.explain: Stonehenge is a circle of huge standing stones in England.

exercises.prompt: Stonehenge's giant stones were raised about 4,500 years ago.
exercises.hint: They were raised about 2500 BC. Add about 2,000 years for AD.
exercises.explain: True: about 2500 BC is about 4,500 years ago.

exercises.hint: It is on Salisbury Plain, in the south of Great Britain.
exercises.explain: Stonehenge is in England, part of the United Kingdom.

exercises.prompt: Stonehenge was built with cranes and trucks.
exercises.hint: When were cranes and trucks invented?
exercises.explain: False: it was built about 4,500 years ago, long before any machines.

exercises.prompt: Where did the smaller bluestones come from?
exercises.hint: They came from far away, in another part of Britain.
exercises.explain: The bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, about 240 km away.

exercises.prompt: How did people probably move the big stones?
exercises.hint: They had wood, rope and lots of people.
choices: on wooden sledges pulled with ropes
exercises.explain: Teams probably pulled them on wooden sledges with ropes, over tracks of wood.

exercises.prompt: Put Stonehenge's story in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: The ditch came about 500 years before the big stones.
items: a round ditch and bank are dug
exercises.explain: The ditch and bank (about 3000 BC), the stones (about 2500 BC), people stop using it, and visitors today.

exercises.prompt: At midsummer, the Sun rises near Stonehenge's Heel Stone.
exercises.hint: Remember how the stones line up with the Sun.
exercises.explain: True: the builders lined the stones up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is still a mystery about Stonehenge?
exercises.hint: Three of these we can see for ourselves today.
choices: that it is made of stone
that its stones stand in a circle
exercises.explain: We can see what it is and where it is, but nobody knows exactly why it was built.

exercises.prompt: How do archaeologists know the builders dug with antler picks?
exercises.hint: The builders left no writing. What else can tell us?
choices: antler picks were found in the holes
exercises.explain: Picks made of deer antler were found in the ditch and the stone holes.

exercises.prompt: Archaeologists know for certain how every stone was moved.
exercises.hint: Remember what is known and what is still a mystery.
exercises.explain: False: they have good ideas, like sledges and ropes, but nobody knows for certain.

exercises.prompt: Why might the builders have lined the stones up with the Sun?
exercises.hint: Farmers needed to know the seasons.
choices: to mark special times of the year
exercises.explain: The stones mark midsummer and midwinter, so the builders may have used them to mark the year.

exercises.prompt: An elephant weighs about 6 tonnes. About how many elephants weigh the same as a 25-tonne stone?
exercises.hint: Count in sixes until you get close to 25.
exercises.explain: 6, 12, 18, 24: about 4 elephants weigh the same as one big sarsen stone.

exercises.prompt: Sort these facts about Stonehenge: known, or still a mystery?
items: when the big stones were raised
exercises.hint: Which ones have clues that archaeologists found, and which do they still argue about?
exercises.explain: Known: when the stones were raised and where the bluestones came from. Still a mystery: exactly why it was built and how every stone was moved.

exercises.prompt: Match each stone to what we know about it.
matches: the midsummer Sun rises by it
exercises.hint: Look back at the cards about the stones and the Sun.
exercises.explain: The sarsens are the biggest, the bluestones came from Wales, and the Sun rises near the Heel Stone at midsummer.

exercises.prompt: The sarsens came about 25 km. The bluestones came about 240 km. How much further did the bluestones come?
exercises.hint: Take the shorter distance from the longer one.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of raising a big stone in order.
items: Lever it up into its hole.
Load the stone onto a wooden sledge.
Pack the hole with earth and stones.
exercises.hint: The stone must reach the site before it can be raised.
exercises.explain: Load the stone onto a sledge, drag it with ropes, lever it up into its hole, then pack the hole so it stands firm.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: what archaeologists found, or what they worked out from clues?
items: bluestone that matches rock in Wales
exercises.hint: Could you hold it in your hand, or is it an idea from the clues?
exercises.explain: Found: antler picks, burials, and bluestone that matches Welsh rock. Worked out: no sledge was found, so sledges are an idea, and so are midwinter gatherings, from clues like the stones lining up with the Sun.
